visuals.thirdEyeAboutText: Long before it was a symbol, the third eye was a claim about the body itself — the pineal gland, which the philosopher René Descartes called "the seat of the soul." In Hindu tradition it is Ajna, the brow chakra of intuition and inner sight; in Buddhist and Theosophical thought it is the eye that opens onto truths ordinary vision cannot reach. Every culture that named it agreed on one thing: somewhere between the eyebrows lies a sense for what the other two eyes cannot see — and once it opens, the world looks different.

decoder.title: DECODE THE DOLLAR
decoder.sub: TAP A NUMBERED POINT TO SEE WHAT IT REALLY MEANS — AND WHAT THE MYTHS GET WRONG.
decoder.caption: Stylised redrawing of the Great Seal's reverse. The Seal was adopted on 20 June 1782 and has been on the one-dollar bill since 1935.
decoder.artLabel: Drawing of the reverse of the Great Seal of the United States with five interactive points

annuit.title: ANNUIT CŒPTIS
annuit.what: Latin for “He has favored our undertakings” — a thank-you to Providence, written above the eye. Count the letters: there are exactly thirteen.
annuit.fact: It sounds like a secret oath, but Thomson's own 1782 explanation is on record: it thanks Providence for the success of the American cause.

eye.title: THE EYE OF PROVIDENCE
eye.what: A radiant eye in a triangle floats above the pyramid. Thomson said the eye and motto “allude to the many signal interpositions of providence in favour of the American cause” — the belief that fortune had smiled on the revolution.
eye.fact: First proposed in 1776 by the artist Pierre Eugène du Simitière, who was not a Freemason. The eye only shows up in Masonic manuals in 1797 — 15 years after the seal — and in Christian art it stood for the Trinity as early as 1525.

pyramid.title: THE UNFINISHED PYRAMID
pyramid.what: Thirteen courses of stone, one for each original state, with the top left open. Designer Charles Thomson told Congress in 1782: “The pyramid signifies Strength and Duration.” The open top is usually read as a nation still being built.
pyramid.fact: The pyramid was William Barton’s idea (1782). Pyramids were a common 18th-century sign of permanence; historians find no evidence linking it to any secret society.

date.title: MDCCLXXVI
date.what: Roman numerals for 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence, carved on the base of the pyramid — the moment the count of thirteen begins.
date.fact: The Bavarian Illuminati were also founded in 1776 (1 May, in Ingolstadt) — a coincidence that fuels a lot of theories. No evidence connects the two events.

novus.title: NOVUS ORDO SECLORUM
novus.what: Borrowed from the Roman poet Virgil: “a new order of the ages.” Thomson explained it marks the beginning of the new American era, counted from 1776.
novus.fact: It is not “New World Order.” The Latin says ordo seclorum — order of the ages — and never mentions the world. The modern phrase came much later.

about.title: ABOUT
about.sub: WHO WE ARE. WHAT THIS IS. WHAT IT IS NOT.
about.intro: Illuminati Brotherhood is an immersive brand and story world about secret-society mythology, conspiracy culture and historical mystery. Nothing here is a claim about any real organisation.

the-third-eye.title: THE THIRD EYE
the-third-eye.desc: A symbol representing knowledge, perception and hidden truth.
the-third-eye.body: Older than any order that claimed it, the open eye appears wherever humans wanted to say "we see more than we are told". In the Brotherhood's story it marks the first chamber: the moment an initiate stops accepting and starts looking.

the-gathering.title: THE GATHERING
the-gathering.desc: Hooded keepers circle the eternal flame of counsel.
the-gathering.body: Thirteen robes, one circle, no faces. The Gathering is the Brotherhood's founding image — a council where rank dissolves and only the flame is above anyone. It is staged and symbolic.

the-golden-altar.title: THE GOLDEN ALTAR
the-golden-altar.desc: Where candlelight meets the triangular gate of awakening.
the-golden-altar.body: A triangle of light set into the stone. Initiates kneel not to worship, but to look through it. The altar is a lens in the story: what you see on the other side is whatever you brought with you.

the-horned-figure.title: THE HORNED FIGURE
the-horned-figure.desc: Myth and allegory guarding the gate of forbidden wisdom.
the-horned-figure.body: Borrowed from centuries of allegory, the horned guardian is the story's antagonist and mirror at once. It represents the fear of knowledge — the thing standing between the seeker and the fourth chamber.

the-threshold.title: THE THRESHOLD
the-threshold.desc: One silhouette. One triangle. One choice to step through.
the-threshold.body: Every initiate reaches a door they can still walk away from. The Threshold is that scene, frozen: the figure, the flame, and the moment before the choice.

the-grimoire.title: THE GRIMOIRE
the-grimoire.desc: Parchments of sigils, circles and centuries-old questions.
the-grimoire.body: The final chamber holds a book that is never finished. Its sigils are the visual language of the whole experience — you will find them hidden across every page of this site.

the-third-eye.name: THE THIRD EYE
the-third-eye.meaning: The eye that sees what is hidden. In the story it is the first mark an initiate receives — the reminder to question everything, including the Brotherhood itself.

the-pyramid.name: THE PYRAMID
the-pyramid.meaning: Wide at the base, narrow at the peak: knowledge is easy to begin and hard to finish. The capstone floats free because the climb is never complete.
the-pyramid.about: The Great Pyramid of Giza stayed the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years, until a medieval English cathedral overtook it. The 13-step 'unfinished pyramid' on the US Great Seal (1782) carries the words Novus Ordo Seclorum, 'a new order of the ages' — but it only reached the dollar bill in 1935.

the-shadow.name: THE SHADOW
the-shadow.meaning: The hooded silhouette stands for every keeper who chose anonymity. Faces are never shown in Brotherhood imagery — the story matters more than the storyteller.
the-shadow.about: Anonymity is as old as secret societies. Adam Weishaupt, who founded the Bavarian Illuminati in 1776, went by the code name 'Spartacus', and his members took classical aliases too. And Masonic candidates traditionally wear a blindfold called a 'hoodwink' — a word that once just meant covering the eyes.

the-horned-figure.name: THE HORNED FIGURE
the-horned-figure.meaning: Borrowed from centuries of allegory and deliberately reframed as the fear of knowledge. The antagonist of the story, and its mirror.
the-horned-figure.about: The name 'Baphomet' first appears in 1307, in the trial records of the Knights Templar — probably a garbled 'Mahomet' written down under torture. The famous goat-headed figure came about 550 years later: Éliphas Lévi drew it in 1856 as a diagram of balanced opposites, human and beast, male and female — not as a devil. It has been misread ever since.

the-black-sun.name: THE BLACK SUN
the-black-sun.meaning: A sun that gives no light, only outline. The emblem of the vigil: the idea that some truths are only visible in darkness.
the-black-sun.about: Alchemists had a black sun of their own: sol niger, the darkest stage of the Great Work, when matter is broken down before it can be reborn. Carl Jung later used the image for the moment a person's old self dissolves. That is why the Vigil is kept at night — the dark stage comes before the change.

the-emblem.name: THE EMBLEM
the-emblem.meaning: Triangle, eye and ring of runes. The seal every initiate receives at the seventh station and the mark that appears on every page of this experience.
the-emblem.about: Seals are older than signatures. Mesopotamian scribes rolled carved cylinder seals across wet clay as early as 3500 BC to prove who had approved something. The Great Seal of the United States took six years and three committees to design (1776–1782) — even a simple emblem can hide a long debate.

the-altar-gate.name: THE ALTAR GATE
the-altar-gate.meaning: The lit triangle set into stone. Not a place of worship but of looking — a lens through which the seeker sees whatever they carried in.
the-altar-gate.about: At Abu Simbel in Egypt, sunlight does something extraordinary twice a year: it travels 60 metres into the mountain and lights three of the four statues in the inner sanctuary. The fourth, Ptah, linked with darkness and the underworld, stays in shadow. Aiming light at the sacred is over 3,000 years old.

the-grimoire-page.name: THE GRIMOIRE PAGE
the-grimoire-page.meaning: Sigils, circles and centuries-old questions. The visual language of the whole experience, drawn from a book that is never finished.
the-grimoire-page.about: The word 'grimoire' comes from the Old French for 'grammar' — a book of learning so powerful it sounded dangerous. The most famous real one may be the Voynich Manuscript: about 240 pages of unknown script and strange plants, carbon-dated to 1404–1438, and still undeciphered. Yale's library has put it online, where anyone can look — and no one can read it.

the-owl-of-minerva.name: THE OWL OF MINERVA
the-owl-of-minerva.meaning: The one emblem with a documented link: Adam Weishaupt's Bavarian Illuminati (1776) took an owl on an open book, after Minerva, goddess of wisdom. In the story it watches over the humblest first grade of every initiate.
the-owl-of-minerva.about: The philosopher Hegel wrote that the owl of Minerva flies only at dusk — wisdom arrives once the day is done. In 1776 Adam Weishaupt's Illuminati chose the owl as their mark, and their entry rank was called 'Minerval'. The order lasted less than ten years: Bavaria banned it in 1785, and the legend has outlived it by two centuries.

the-hexagram.name: THE HEXAGRAM
the-hexagram.meaning: Two interlocked triangles, fire rising and water descending. An ancient figure found in alchemy, architecture and many faiths — here, opposites held in balance.
the-hexagram.about: Two triangles — one pointing up for fire, one down for water. Alchemists drew the hexagram as the marriage of opposites. The same figure goes by many names: the Seal of Solomon, the Star of David, and in India the Shatkona, the union of Shiva and Shakti. Few shapes have been claimed by so many traditions at once.

the-rose-cross.name: THE ROSE CROSS
the-rose-cross.meaning: The emblem of the 17th-century Rosicrucian manifestos, about a brotherhood that may never have existed. A rose at the heart of a cross: mystery blooming inside structure.
the-rose-cross.about: In 1614 a pamphlet appeared in Germany announcing a secret brotherhood of wise healers who had guarded knowledge for centuries. Two more manifestos followed by 1616, and all of Europe went looking for the Rosicrucians. Historians still can't say whether the Brotherhood ever existed — or whether it was a hoax, a game, or an idea that simply wanted to be believed.

the-obelisk.name: THE OBELISK
the-obelisk.meaning: Egyptian sun-pillars carried by empires to Rome, Paris and Washington. In the story, it marks the spot where an initiate's oath is spoken aloud.
the-obelisk.about: Rome has 13 ancient obelisks — more than any other city on Earth. Emperors shipped them across the Mediterranean as trophies. The Luxor obelisk in Paris is over 3,000 years old, and the Washington Monument is an obelisk too. The originals had gilded tips, made to flash in the first light of dawn.

the-flower-of-life.name: THE FLOWER OF LIFE
the-flower-of-life.meaning: Overlapping circles found on ancient temple walls and in modern sacred-geometry art. In the story it is the map of how every question leads to the next.
the-flower-of-life.about: Nineteen circles of equal size, each passing through the centres of its neighbours — a pattern so regular that people keep finding it: at Egypt's temple of Abydos (scholars still debate its age), in temples across Asia, and in Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks. Start with one circle, add six, and you get the 'Seed of Life', which many read as a picture of creation.

the-skull.name: THE SKULL
the-skull.meaning: A reminder of mortality used by monks, painters and college societies alike. In the story it is not a threat but a question: what will you do with the time you have?
the-skull.about: Memento mori — 'remember you must die' — is one of the oldest ideas in art. Painters hid skulls in portraits, a Roman crypt is decorated with the bones of thousands of Capuchin friars, and Yale's Skull and Bones society (1832) made it a badge. Behind the shudder is a hopeful note: if time is short, every choice counts.

the-sun-and-moon.name: THE SUN & MOON
the-sun-and-moon.meaning: Alchemy's paired luminaries, and a fixture on the ceilings of Masonic lodges. Day and night, reason and dream: the two lights an initiate learns to read by.
the-sun-and-moon.about: Alchemists gave every metal a heavenly body: gold to the Sun, silver to the Moon, pictured as a king and queen whose 'chemical wedding' produced the Philosopher's Stone. In Freemasonry the Sun, the Moon and the Master of the Lodge are the 'three lesser lights'. In old symbolism, day and night are never rivals — always partners.

the-pentagram.name: THE PENTAGRAM
the-pentagram.meaning: Drawn in a single unbroken stroke, it was a Pythagorean sign of health and later a symbol of the human body. Pop culture flipped its meaning; the story restores it: one perfect closed line.
the-pentagram.about: Draw it without lifting your pen and every crossing divides the lines in the golden ratio — which is why the Pythagoreans, devoted to number, used it as a secret sign of recognition and named it Hygieia, 'health'. Venus plays along too: over eight years its meetings with the Sun trace a rough five-pointed star across the sky.

eye-of-providence.name: EYE OF PROVIDENCE
eye-of-providence.meaning: A radiant eye set inside a triangle, inked on every Keeper's wrist at the Council. In the story it marks a vow of vigilance — not a claim about any real order.

silent-owl.name: THE SILENT OWL
silent-owl.meaning: Worn between the shoulder blades by the story's oldest members, the owl marks those who listen more than they speak. An emblem of quiet observation.

twin-pillars.name: THE TWIN PILLARS
twin-pillars.meaning: Two columns, light and shadow, always inked as a pair. In the story they represent the balance every initiate must hold between question and answer.

compass-square.name: COMPASS & SQUARE
compass-square.meaning: A measuring tool turned emblem — the compass for vision, the square for conduct. In the story it is given only after the Sealed Oath.

checkered-floor.name: THE CHECKERED FLOOR
checkered-floor.meaning: Light and dark tiles inked as a band around the wrist, a reminder that every choice in the story has its opposite.

ouroboros.name: THE OUROBOROS
ouroboros.meaning: A serpent devouring its own tail, marking those who complete a full cycle of the seven stations. Worn only after the Crossing.

thirteen-steps.name: THE THIRTEEN STEPS
thirteen-steps.meaning: A stepped pyramid with a floating capstone, one line for each step. The 'unfinished pyramid' of the US Great Seal has thirteen steps, one per original colony. In the story: thirteen chambers, none ever completed.

coiled-serpent.name: THE COILED SERPENT
coiled-serpent.meaning: A serpent in a slow S-curve, inked along the forearm. Ancient across cultures as both danger and renewal; in the story it marks initiates who have shed their first belief.

anubis.name: THE JACKAL GUIDE
anubis.meaning: Anubis, the jackal-headed Egyptian guide of the dead, drawn in profile. Chosen by people who want protection at thresholds; in the story he leads the initiate through the Crossing.

metatrons-cube.name: METATRON'S CUBE
metatrons-cube.meaning: Thirteen circles joined by straight lines, a favourite of sacred-geometry tattoo artists. In the story it is the council's diagram: twelve keepers around one empty seat.

double-eagle.name: THE DOUBLE EAGLE
double-eagle.meaning: Two heads facing opposite ways, the emblem of the Scottish Rite's 33rd degree and of several old empires. In the story: one eye on the past, one on what comes next.

lotus-eye.name: THE LOTUS EYE
lotus-eye.meaning: An eye opening at the heart of a lotus — the third eye of Eastern tradition given petals. In the story it is inked over the sternum by those who finish the Vigil.

hourglass.name: THE HOURGLASS
hourglass.meaning: Time as a two-chambered vessel, a reminder from painters and lodge-halls that the sand runs one way. In the story it is the mark of the First Candle: one hour, no speaking.

xiii-numeral.name: THE NUMERAL XIII
xiii-numeral.meaning: Thirteen in Roman numerals — thirteen steps, thirteen seats, thirteen chambers. Inked small, behind the ear or on the wrist, by those who love number-lore.

the-key.name: THE KEEPER'S KEY
the-key.meaning: An old iron key with a trefoil bow. Keys appear in Rosicrucian and Masonic imagery as the right to open what is closed. In the story the Grand Keeper hands one to each sealed initiate.

discord.name: DISCORD

origin.title: A story, not a claim
origin.text: The Brotherhood began as a creative project: what if secret-society mythology were treated as cinema instead of conspiracy?

archive.title: Six chambers
archive.text: The Ritual Archive gave the story a structure — six relics, six chambers, one journey from perception to oath.

council.title: The community
council.text: Initiates joined the round table. Their theories, art and questions now shape where the story goes next.

newOrder.title: The New Order
newOrder.text: On 31 December 2026 at 11:59:59 PM IST the counter hits zero and the next chapter opens. Scheduled, and entirely ours.

isReal.a: The history we cite is real. The Brotherhood itself — its rituals, council, countdown and lore — is our own creation, a story world inspired by secret-society symbolism. We are not affiliated with any real organisation.

whoCanJoin.a: Anyone who enjoys mystery, cinema and mythology. You must be 18 or older, because some visuals are dark and mature in tone.

accountDoes.a: Signed-in initiates unlock sealed videos and rituals and receive an initiate number. Admins (Keepers) manage members and sealed content.

realWorldClaims.q: Do you make real-world claims about people or organisations?
realWorldClaims.a: Never. Any resemblance to real people, groups or events is coincidental or purely referential for the sake of the story.
